context_blurb:
Some things you could do on the day you were born, and some you had to learn. A behaviour that no one has to teach is an instinct: a living thing is born with it, and every member of its kind does it the same way. A learned behaviour comes from experience, such as practice, watching others or a reward. Both kinds help living things survive.

People are born with instincts. Press a finger into a newborn baby's palm, and her tiny fingers curl tight around it. She can grip like this from her very first day, with no lessons at all. This grip is a reflex, an action the body does by itself, and it fades by about six months.

Some reflexes last a lifetime and keep you safe. A sneeze blasts dust from your nose, a cough clears a crumb from your throat, and your hand jerks back from a hot pan before you can think. Looking both ways before crossing a road is a learned skill instead: grown-ups teach children to look both ways, and then once more, before stepping into the street.

Many animals have instincts as well. A garden spider's mother dies in late autumn, soon after laying her eggs. In spring her young hatch, drift off on silk threads, and each spins a wheel-shaped web of its own. No one teaches a young spider, and it has never watched a web being made, yet its web works: it was born knowing how.

A mother sea turtle lays her eggs in a beach nest at night, covers them with sand and goes back to the sea. The eggs hatch about two months later. Because the mother left long before her babies hatched, no one is there to show them the way. Each hatchling crawls toward the brightest part of the sky, which on a dark beach lies over the water.

Learned behaviours are different. When a pet dog learns to sit or give a paw, its owner hands it a treat or praise each time it does the trick, until it does the trick whenever it is told. The dog's puppies are not born knowing the trick, because a learned behaviour is not inherited.

Learning has one more strength. Milk once came to the door in glass bottles, with the cream on top under a thin foil cap. Blue tits, which are small birds, learned to peck through the foil and sip the cream. No instinct could have prepared them for that, yet the trick spread from bird to bird to more than two hundred places. An instinct stays the same, but learning lets animals change their ways as the world around them changes.

Some traits come from genes, passed down to every child from both parents. Eye colour is one of these inherited traits, so a girl adopted as a tiny baby and raised in a faraway land still has eyes coloured by her birth parents' genes. Her language comes from the family who raised her, a skill comes from practice, and a scar from an old fall. Things gained during life are not passed on to children. The scientist August Weismann tested this: he cut the tails off mice, and their young were never born with short tails.
